s: Welcome back to Word Kitchen, everyone.
Today's menu is rich and emotional.
We're serving ten advanced words about emotions and character, the words that describe how people feel, how they behave, and how they carry themselves through life.
Equanimity is calm, balanced composure even when everything around you is falling apart.
Picture a surgeon in an emergency room.
The alarms are blaring, the stakes are life and death, and she keeps her equanimity.
I love equanimity because it's contagious.
A leader with real equanimity steadies the whole team.
Last year my manager handled a disastrous product launch with remarkable equanimity, and honestly, her equanimity is what stopped the rest of us from panicking.
When one person holds their equanimity, the room borrows it.
Diplomats need equanimity during tense negotiations.
The ambassador's equanimity during those long nights of talks genuinely impressed both sides.
A magnanimous person is generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone who has wronged them.
After a bitter election, the winning candidate gave a magnanimous speech, praising her opponent and inviting him to help shape the new policy.
That magnanimous gesture healed a divided country faster than any law could.
It's easy to be generous when you're comfortable.
A magnanimous leader forgives public criticism and still promotes the critic.
I try to be magnanimous in arguments with my brother, though I'll admit my magnanimous moments are rarer than I'd like.
An obstinate person stubbornly refuses to change their mind or course, even when the evidence is against them.
My grandfather was obstinate about his old car.
Mechanics begged him to retire it, but he stayed obstinate.
There's a fine line between principled and obstinate.
The committee chair was so obstinate about the original plan that the reform stalled for a year.
Her obstinate refusal to hear new data frustrated everyone.
The scientist was obstinate in defending her hypothesis, and she turned out to be right.
Sometimes an obstinate streak is just conviction wearing work boots.
A reticent person is reserved, reluctant to speak freely about their thoughts or feelings.
My neighbor is lovely but reticent.
It took three years before she told me anything personal.
Reticent people aren't cold; they're careful.
The usually reticent novelist surprised everyone by publishing a painfully honest memoir.
Interviewers who expected a reticent guest got the most open conversation of the year.
I was reticent about my promotion at first, not wanting to seem boastful.
But being reticent became lonely, so I finally told my friends.
Have you ever been reticent about good news, Maya?
Mercurial describes someone subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood.
Brilliant one minute, furious the next.
Monday he'd praise my article as genius, Tuesday he'd call the same draft a disaster.
Working for a mercurial manager taught me to never take either mood personally.
Artists are often called mercurial, though that's a bit of a stereotype.
The conductor's mercurial temperament made every rehearsal electric.
One moment he'd stop the orchestra to weep at a beautiful phrase, the next he'd demand they play it again, harder.
I think we all have mercurial days.
My energy is mercurial before coffee.
Effusive means expressing feelings with overwhelming enthusiasm and warmth.
The critics were effusive after the premiere, calling it the most electrifying performance of the decade.
Their effusive praise filled three pages of the morning paper.
My aunt writes the most effusive birthday cards, full of underlines and exclamation marks.
When she hugs you, it's an effusive, whole-body hug.
Her effusive warmth makes every family gathering better.
There's a difference between effusive and fake.
Effusive joy is real; you can feel it.
When the team won the championship, the fans were effusive in the streets, singing until sunrise.
A stoic person endures hardship without complaint, calmly accepting what they cannot change.
The marathon runner was stoic about her injury, finishing the race on a sprained ankle without a word of complaint.
That stoic determination inspired the whole crowd.
The nurse remained stoic through the hardest night of the outbreak, holding patients' hands while hiding her own exhaustion.
My grandmother was stoic in the old sense.
She raised four kids through a war and never once described herself as suffering.
There's something deeply admirable about that stoic grace.
Impetuous means acting quickly without careful thought.
Rash, impulsive, leaping before you look.
His impetuous decision to quit his job and move abroad with no plan shocked everyone.
That impetuous leap worked out, but it could easily have been a disaster.
The impetuous young trader risked the firm's money on a hunch and lost a fortune.
An impetuous apology can also backfire, by the way, saying sorry before you understand what you did wrong.
I've sent some impetuous text messages in my time.
My rule now: write the impetuous draft, sleep on it, delete it in the morning.
Sanguine means optimistic, especially in the face of difficulty.
Confident that things will work out.
Despite the gloomy economic forecasts, the analysts remain sanguine about long-term growth.
Their sanguine outlook is based on decades of data, not wishful thinking.
Doctors often stay deliberately sanguine with patients.
The surgeon's sanguine tone before the operation calmed the whole family.
Being sanguine isn't naive; it's a choice to focus on what's possible.
I'm trying to be more sanguine.
My default is anxious planning, but a sanguine friend of mine talks me down.
Her sanguine attitude reminds me that most crises pass.
Last word, and it's a spicy one: truculent.
Truculent means aggressively defiant, eager to argue, ready for a fight.
The debate turned truculent when one panelist started shouting over every rebuttal.
His truculent tone killed any chance of real discussion.
The truculent customer at the cafe wasn't really angry about the coffee; he was having a terrible day.
Still, nobody enjoys a truculent confrontation.
Sports crowds can turn truculent fast.
The referee made one bad call and the truculent chanting started.
Security had to step in before the truculent mood spread further.
Lena, give me a sentence with equanimity and obstinate together.
The mediator kept her equanimity even when the obstinate delegates refused every compromise.
She gave a magnanimous reply to his truculent email, and he actually apologized.
He's reticent with strangers but effusive with his grandchildren.
Her mood is mercurial, but her work ethic is stoic.
His impetuous investments worry me, though he's sanguine they'll pay off.
That's our ten: equanimity, magnanimous, obstinate, reticent, mercurial, effusive, stoic, impetuous, sanguine, and truculent.
And notice how they pair up.
Thanks for cooking with us on Word Kitchen.
See you tomorrow, and stay sanguine out there.
